Honestly, my issues are the exact opposite—I'm incredibly disorganized, constantly losing my keys or wallet, and forgetting things rather than checking or arranging them.\n\nDoctor: Do you often act on impulse, doing things without much thought, like blurting out answers or interrupting others, and do you have difficulty waiting for your turn in lines or conversations?\n\nPatient: Yes, I do, and it's really embarrassing—I constantly cut people off and blurt out what I think they're going to say before they can finish. I also get incredibly impatient waiting in lines or waiting my turn to speak in discussions, to the point where I'm practically biting my tongue to keep from jumping in.\n\nDoctor: Can you tell me more about your experience with making careless mistakes or failing to follow through on instructions, and how that compares to your impulsivity and restlessness?\n\nPatient: On the inattentive side, I make careless mistakes like missing a minus sign in my code or skipping fields on forms, and my brain just 'lets go of the thread' halfway through a project. But contrasted with that, the restlessness feels like a physical buzzing under my skin that makes me constantly pace, fidget, and impatiently blurt things out because waiting is so unbearable. It's incredibly frustrating because I'm either drifting off mentally or physically unable to slow down.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe how often you experience significant feelings of restlessness or fidgeting in quiet environments, compared to your difficulties with sustaining focus or following through on tasks?\n\nPatient: Both happen almost constantly, but they feel very different. In quiet environments, I get a physical buzzing under my skin within minutes, forcing me to fidget, shake my leg, or pace because sitting quietly feels unbearable. In contrast, my focus issues feel like my brain constantly losing the thread of a task and getting pulled away by any tiny distraction, leaving projects completely unfinished.\n\nDoctor: Do you find that your difficulties with restlessness and fidgeting, or your issues with sustaining focus and following through on tasks, cause you more problems in your daily life and relationships?\n\nPatient: While both are definitely major issues, the difficulties with sustaining focus and following through on tasks have caused much more severe problems in my life. My restlessness is annoying and makes it hard to relax, but the lack of follow-through is what actually cost me my job, caused me to miss critical deadlines, and made me pull back socially out of shame after letting down friends and mentors.\n\nDoctor: Can you estimate the age when you first started noticing these difficulties with focus and restlessness, and have they been relatively consistent over time or have you noticed any significant changes?\n\nPatient: These issues actually go all the way back to elementary school, where my report cards always noted I was \"bright but daydreams, forgets homework, and talks out of turn.\" While these patterns have been consistent, they really came to a head over the last year when my responsibilities ramped up at the startup and my old coping mechanisms stopped working.\n\nDoctor: Can you tell me if your restlessness and fidgeting are more pronounced in certain situations or environments, such as at work or in social settings?\n\nPatient: It happens in almost all environments, but it's especially bad when I'm forced to sit still for more than a few minutes—like in waiting rooms or lectures—where I get a physical buzzing feeling and just have to fidget or pace. Even in relaxed social settings with my roommates, I can't just sit and watch a show; I'm constantly checking my phone, jumping up, or starting random tasks because staying quiet feels unbearable.\n\nDoctor: Can you compare the severity of your symptoms of inattention, such as difficulty sustaining focus and following through on tasks, to your symptoms of hyperactivity and impulsivity, such as restlessness and blurting out answers, in terms of how much they interfere with your daily functioning and relationships?\n\nPatient: While both are constant, the inattention and follow-through issues have had a far more severe impact on my life. My restlessness and tendency to blurt things out make me feel self-conscious and worry about annoying others, but my struggles to finish tasks, stay organized, and remember commitments are what actually cost me my startup job, stalled my career, and led to me letting down my friends.\n\nDoctor: Would you say that your difficulties with inattention and follow-through have consistently caused more significant problems in your daily life and relationships compared to your symptoms of restlessness and impulsivity?\n\nPatient: Yes, absolutely. While the restlessness and blurting things out are frustrating and embarrassing, it's the inability to follow through, stay organized, and remember daily tasks that has caused the most damage. That is what actually cost me my job, caused me to miss deadlines, and led me to pull back socially after letting down my friends and mentors.\n\nDoctor: Can you clarify if there was ever a period in your life where your symptoms of hyperactivity and impulsivity, such as restlessness and blurting out answers, were more prominent than your symptoms of inattention, or have your inattention symptoms always been the more significant issue?\n\nPatient: I'm not quite sure if one was ever more prominent than the other, as I feel like both the restlessness and the inattention have been present since I was a kid. They have always coexisted, though the trouble with focus and finishing tasks is definitely what has caused the most severe, life-disrupting problems for me recently.\n\nDoctor: Looking back over your life, have there been periods where you experienced significant symptoms of hyperactivity and impulsivity without notable inattention, or have inattention symptoms always been a major part of your experience?\n\nPatient: Inattention has always been a major part of my experience alongside the hyperactivity and impulsivity, rather than them existing as separate phases. Even looking back to elementary school, my report cards and memories show a constant mix of both—I was always daydreaming, losing worksheets, and forgetting homework right alongside talking out of turn and blurting out answers.\n\nDoctor: You've mentioned that both hyperactivity and inattention have been present since childhood, but can you think of any situations or periods in your life where one set of symptoms clearly overshadowed the other, even if briefly?\n\nPatient: I'm not really sure, and I can't recall any specific period where one set of symptoms clearly overshadowed the other. For as long as I can remember, the scatterbrained, inattentive side and the restless, fidgety side have always seemed to go hand-in-hand. They have just always coexisted together.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel that your symptoms of inattention, such as difficulty sustaining focus and following through on tasks, have consistently been more problematic for you than your symptoms of hyperactivity and impulsivity, such as restlessness and blurting out answers, throughout your life?\n\nPatient: I'm not quite sure or haven't really thought about comparing them that way throughout my whole life. Both the focus issues and the restlessness have caused different kinds of problems for me over the years, so it's hard to say one has consistently been worse than the other.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever experienced a time when you were able to control your restlessness and impulsivity, but still struggled with inattention and following through on tasks, or vice versa?"

It's incredibly frustrating because I'm either drifting off mentally or physically unable to slow down.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe how often you experience significant feelings of restlessness or fidgeting in quiet environments, compared to your difficulties with sustaining focus or following through on tasks?\n\nPatient: Both happen almost constantly, but they feel very different. Both the focus issues and the restlessness have caused different kinds of problems for me over the years, so it's hard to say one has consistently been worse than the other.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever experienced a time when you were able to control your restlessness and impulsivity, but still struggled with inattention and following through on tasks, or vice versa?\n\nPatient: I haven't really noticed a time when one set of symptoms was controlled while the other wasn't. Even when I was younger or in college and managing to get by, it was never \"without difficulty\"—I was still constantly daydreaming, losing assignments, and relying on last-minute panic to finish tasks, all while feeling restless and blurting things out.\n\nDoctor: Looking back, do you think your difficulties with restlessness and impulsivity have been as consistently problematic for you as your difficulties with inattention and following through on tasks, or have they varied in impact over time?\n\nPatient: Both have been present since childhood, like getting in trouble for daydreaming and losing worksheets alongside blurting out answers in elementary school. Meanwhile, the restlessness and impulsivity have remained a consistent, annoying \"buzz\" in the background rather than causing a sudden crisis.\n\nDoctor: Do you think there was ever a distinct period in your life where you only experienced symptoms of inattention without significant restlessness and impulsivity, or vice versa?\n\nPatient: No, I don't think there was ever a separate period like that. For as long as I can remember, even going back to elementary school, my daydreaming and forgetting homework always went hand-in-hand with my talking out of turn and blurting things out. They have always co-existed rather than occurring in separate, distinct phases of my life.\n\nDoctor: Have you noticed any significant changes in the severity or impact of your inattention symptoms compared to your hyperactivity and impulsivity symptoms as you've grown older, or have they remained relatively consistent in how they affect your daily life?\n\nPatient: I'm not entirely sure, and I haven't really thought about comparing their severity over time that way. Both types of struggles have been there since I was a kid, though the focus and organization issues have definitely caused the most obvious, severe problems recently with my job and career.\n\nDoctor: Can you estimate the frequency or proportion of times when you feel like your hyperactivity and impulsivity symptoms are more bothersome to you compared to the times when your inattention symptoms are more bothersome?\n\nPatient: I'm not really sure how to estimate an exact proportion or percentage, as I've never really thought about it that way before. Both types of struggles feel constantly present and frustrating in their own ways, so it's hard to break down which one bothers me more often.\n\nDoctor: Looking back on your life, do you feel that the difficulties with focus and following through on tasks have been the primary issue causing problems, or have the symptoms of restlessness and impulsivity been equally disruptive to your daily functioning and relationships?\n\nPatient: Both have definitely been disruptive, but in very different ways. And if I have to sit still or try to relax quietly, I get this buzzing feeling under my skin that makes it feel unbearable, so I'm constantly fidgeting or pacing.\n\nDoctor: Do you also experience recurring, unwanted thoughts or urges to perform specific rituals or behaviors, like checking things multiple times or arranging items in a particular way?\n\nPatient: No, I don't really experience anything like that or feel the need to perform rituals or keep things neat. Honestly, my issues are the exact opposite—I'm incredibly disorganized, constantly losing my keys or wallet, and forgetting things rather than checking or arranging them.\n\nDoctor: Do you often act on impulse, doing things without much thought, like blurting out answers or interrupting others, and do you have difficulty waiting for your turn in lines or conversations?\n\nPatient: Yes, I do, and it's really embarrassing—I constantly cut people off and blurt out what I think they're going to say before they can finish. I also get incredibly impatient waiting in lines or waiting my turn to speak in discussions, to the point where I'm practically biting my tongue to keep from jumping in.\n\nDoctor: Can you tell me more about your experience with making careless mistakes or failing to follow through on instructions, and how that compares to your impulsivity and restlessness?\n\nPatient: On the inattentive side, I make careless mistakes like missing a minus sign in my code or skipping fields on forms, and my brain just 'lets go of the thread' halfway through a project. I'm just really trying to understand why I can't seem to complete things despite having the motivation and ability.\n\nDoctor: Do you often find yourself getting easily distracted, or having trouble sitting still and quietly, even in situations where you're supposed to be focused?\n\nPatient: Yes, definitely. The tiniest distraction, like a notification or a random thought, completely derails me and sends me down a rabbit hole on my phone. Honestly, my issues are the exact opposite—I'm incredibly disorganized, constantly losing my keys or wallet, and forgetting things rather than checking or arranging them.\n\nDoctor: Do you often act on impulse, doing things without much thought, like blurting out answers or interrupting others, and do you have difficulty waiting for your turn in lines or conversations?\n\nPatient: Yes, I do, and it's really embarrassing—I constantly cut people off and blurt out what I think they're going to say before they can finish. I also get incredibly impatient waiting in lines or waiting my turn to speak in discussions, to the point where I'm practically biting my tongue to keep from jumping in.\n\nDoctor: Can you tell me more about your experience with making careless mistakes or failing to follow through on instructions, and how that compares to your impulsivity and restlessness?\n\nPatient: On the inattentive side, I make careless mistakes like missing a minus sign in my code or skipping fields on forms, and my brain just 'lets go of the thread' halfway through a project. My restlessness is annoying and makes it hard to relax, but the lack of follow-through is what actually cost me my job, caused me to miss critical deadlines, and made me pull back socially out of shame after letting down friends and mentors.\n\nDoctor: Can you estimate the age when you first started noticing these difficulties with focus and restlessness, and have they been relatively consistent over time or have you noticed any significant changes?\n\nPatient: These issues actually go all the way back to elementary school, where my report cards always noted I was \"bright but daydreams, forgets homework, and talks out of turn.\" While these patterns have been consistent, they really came to a head over the last year when my responsibilities ramped up at the startup and my old coping mechanisms stopped working.\n\nDoctor: Can you tell me if your restlessness and fidgeting are more pronounced in certain situations or environments, such as at work or in social settings?\n\nPatient: It happens in almost all environments, but it's especially bad when I'm forced to sit still for more than a few minutes—like in waiting rooms or lectures—where I get a physical buzzing feeling and just have to fidget or pace. Even in relaxed social settings with my roommates, I can't just sit and watch a show; I'm constantly checking my phone, jumping up, or starting random tasks because staying quiet feels unbearable.\n\nDoctor: Can you compare the severity of your symptoms of inattention, such as difficulty sustaining focus and following through on tasks, to your symptoms of hyperactivity and impulsivity, such as restlessness and blurting out answers, in terms of how much they interfere with your daily functioning and relationships?\n\nPatient: While both are constant, the inattention and follow-through issues have had a far more severe impact on my life. My restlessness and tendency to blurt things out make me feel self-conscious and worry about annoying others, but my struggles to finish tasks, stay organized, and remember commitments are what actually cost me my startup job, stalled my career, and led to me letting down my friends.\n\nDoctor: Would you say that your difficulties with inattention and follow-through have consistently caused more significant problems in your daily life and relationships compared to your symptoms of restlessness and impulsivity?\n\nPatient: Yes, absolutely. While the restlessness and blurting things out are frustrating and embarrassing, it's the inability to follow through, stay organized, and remember daily tasks that has caused the most damage. That is what actually cost me my job, caused me to miss deadlines, and led me to pull back socially after letting down my friends and mentors.\n\nDoctor: Can you clarify if there was ever a period in your life where your symptoms of hyperactivity and impulsivity, such as restlessness and blurting out answers, were more prominent than your symptoms of inattention, or have your inattention symptoms always been the more significant issue?\n\nPatient: I'm not quite sure if one was ever more prominent than the other, as I feel like both the restlessness and the inattention have been present since I was a kid. They have always coexisted, though the trouble with focus and finishing tasks is definitely what has caused the most severe, life-disrupting problems for me recently.\n\nDoctor: Looking back over your life, have there been periods where you experienced significant symptoms of hyperactivity and impulsivity without notable inattention, or have inattention symptoms always been a major part of your experience?\n\nPatient: Inattention has always been a major part of my experience alongside the hyperactivity and impulsivity, rather than them existing as separate phases. For as long as I can remember, the scatterbrained, inattentive side and the restless, fidgety side have always seemed to go hand-in-hand. They have just always coexisted together.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel that your symptoms of inattention, such as difficulty sustaining focus and following through on tasks, have consistently been more problematic for you than your symptoms of hyperactivity and impulsivity, such as restlessness and blurting out answers, throughout your life?\n\nPatient: I'm not quite sure or haven't really thought about comparing them that way throughout my whole life. However, the inattention and follow-through issues became much more destructive over the last year as my responsibilities grew, ultimately costing me my job. Both types of struggles have been there since I was a kid, though the focus and organization issues have definitely caused the most obvious, severe problems recently with my job and career.\n\nDoctor: Can you estimate the frequency or proportion of times when you feel like your hyperactivity and impulsivity symptoms are more bothersome to you compared to the times when your inattention symptoms are more bothersome?\n\nPatient: I'm not really sure how to estimate an exact proportion or percentage, as I've never really thought about it that way before. Both types of struggles feel constantly present and frustrating in their own ways, so it's hard to break down which one bothers me more often.\n\nDoctor: Looking back on your life, do you feel that the difficulties with focus and following through on tasks have been the primary issue causing problems, or have the symptoms of restlessness and impulsivity been equally disruptive to your daily functioning and relationships?\n\nPatient: Both have definitely been disruptive, but in very different ways.
